caption_chunks.context: the system model of the onboard computer as an example. A shared library, KronOS, serves as middleware between the RTOS and the process logic. The interfaces between software layers are defined through well-specified APIs, and all available hardware interfaces are documented. Each subsystem is further divided into modules, where each module is dedicated to a specific task and provides an API to other software modules. The modules within the KronOS library are optional and can be included or excluded depending on system requirements. caption_chunks.caption: Fig. 3 KronOS Software Layers
caption_chunks.context: A Real-Time Operating System provides the deterministic behaviour that a critical system requires to meet hard deadlines. The design philosophy behind the UWE-5 embedded software strives to achieve welldefined layers that perform functionalities and/or services to the other layers. The mission code layer is separated from the RTOS layer using an Operating System Abstraction Layer (OSAL), which is composed of the well-known POSIX threading APIs (pthreads) [13]. A special layer, called the KronOS Task-Manager, extends the FreeRTOS scheduler with functionality for dynamic resource allocation, load balancing, and fault management. elements.name: The Neutron-2 mission aims to study neutron and gamma-ray fluxes as a function of time, geomagnetic position (lat, lon, alt), and solar activity to gain insights into cosmic ray interactions, solar particle events, and space weather in LEO to make space exploration safer for all.
MO-1: Measure the flux of secondary neutrons and gamma rays produced by cosmic ray interactions in Low Earth Orbit as a function of time, geomagnetic latitude, and altitude (location based data).
MO-2: Measure secondary neutron and gamma ray flux variations before, during, and after solar energetic particle (SEP) events (event based data).

MSC-1: The mission shall collect neutron fluxes over one of Earth’s poles (latitudes >66°N or <−66°S), subdivided into three latitude bands: 66°–74°, 74°–82°, and 82°–90°. The accumulated neutron count within each band must have a maximum relative uncertainty of 10% (TBC).

FSC-1: The mission shall collect at least two sets of 10,000 accumulated neutron counts in each of the following regions: the North Pole, the South Pole (Latitudes >66°N and <−66°S), and the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), with each set separated by at least 3-6 months to enable temporal analysis of the neutron environment in low Earth orbit.

ESC-1: The mission shall collect at least 10,000 accumulated neutron counts in each of the following regions: the North Pole, the South Pole, and the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), at two different altitudes separated by at least 50 km (at least 60,000 counts total). The two altitude-based data sets for each region shall be collected within 40 days of each other.

MSC-2: Collect neutron and gamma ray flux before, during, and after a single solar energetic particle (SEP) event. For the SEP event of interest, the 'before' and 'after' data must be collected within 40 days of the event, and no other SEP event should occur between the 'before' and 'after' data periods.

FSC-2: Collect neutron and gamma ray flux before, during, and after at least two distinct solar energetic particle (SEP) events during the mission. For each SEP event of interest, the 'before' and 'after' data must be collected within 40 days of the event, and no other SEP event should occur between the 'before' and 'after' data periods.

caption_chunks.caption: Figure 2.5. SysML diagram categories supporting MBSE (No Magic, 2022).
caption_chunks.context: SysML supports diverse viewpoints through nine diagram types grouped into four primary categories: structure, behavior, requirements, and parametrics. Figure 2.5 shows the hierarchical classification of these diagram types, each supporting different aspects of the system specification and lifecycle alignment (No Magic, 2022). For example, Block Definition Diagrams (BDDs) and Internal Block Diagrams (IBDs) are used to describe static structure and internal interactions. In contrast, Activity, Sequence, and State Machine diagrams describe dynamic behaviors across operational scenarios.

caption_chunks.context: The modeling constructs in SysML facilitate traceability across stakeholder needs, functional behavior, logical structure, and verification procedures. As shown in Figure 2.6, each diagram type conveys a specific modeling aspect; requirements diagrams capture formalized stakeholder needs, parametric diagrams represent system constraints and analytical expressions, and structural diagrams define system composition and interfaces. In contrast, behavioral diagrams illustrate system dynamics, control logic, and operational workflows (Nonsiri, 2015). Together, these diagrams allow systems engineers to simulate, validate, and iterate system logic in a digital environment before committing to implementation.

caption_chunks.caption: Figure 3.2. MBSE Environment Supporting Digital Thread Integration (Source: Alamy).
caption_chunks.context: The foundation of the Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach in this study lies in its ability to replace document-centric practices with an integrated, model-centric strategy that enhances system fidelity, lifecycle traceability, and cross-domain coherence. MBSE enables the formal specification of system structure, behavior, and requirements through SysML, providing a unified architecture framework that spans stakeholders, engineering domains, and disciplines. By capturing abstractions using standardized constructs, such as blocks, value types, ports, interfaces, and constraints, MBSE supports end-to-end alignment of design intent, verification strategy, and stakeholder expectations.

caption_chunks.context: To manage complexity and uncertainty, a hybrid prioritization approach is employed that combines qualitative assessments with quantitative evaluations. Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA), trade space exploration, and scenario-based simulations are applied through modeling mechanisms, including custom requirement stereotypes, prioritization matrices, and simulation-informed ranking adjustments. analysis.summary: Radar chart comparing prioritization approaches across multiple performance criteria.

caption_chunks.caption: Figure 3.9. Performance-Based Comparison of Prioritization Approaches.
caption_chunks.context: For SidSat, the emphasis is on methods that align with iterative, model-based environments. Techniques such as the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Quality Function Deployment (QFD), Binary Search Tree (BST), and MoSCoW provide structured methods for comparing needs based on utility, feasibility, or complexity (Millet, 2005). While AHP is valued for its pairwise comparisons and transparency, it does not offer native support for feedback loops or direct integration with system modeling tools, such as SysML. Similarly, QFD captures user needs well but presents challenges when applied to architectures that evolve frequently or require rapid validation cycles.

caption_chunks.context: The following Internal Block Diagram (IBD) defines the architecture of the Electrical Power Subsystem II (EPSII), emphasizing the flow of energy from generation to regulated distribution (NASA, 2020). Solar panels and batteries connect through multiple voltage buses, 3.3V, 5V, 12V, and Vbat, establishing a robust multi-source system (CubeSat Program, 2020). Power Distribution Management regulates output to key interfaces and prevents overload conditions (Object Management Group, 2017). Labeled ports are used for solar input (sPIn), battery input (powerIn), and power delivery. A kill switch is included to support subsystem isolation and fault handling in the event of anomalies (INCOSE, 2015).

Within the MBSE framework, the SysML (Systems Modeling Language) can be exploited in order to better define the CubeSat system highlighting its parts or units, and their corresponding requirements. This also allows to better identify: the interconnections between subsystems, and test cases to visualize how a hacker can start an attack and interact with others system blocks. In [8], it is reported an example of SysML application for a crewed Mars mission (exploiting the Cameo Systems Modeler environment), where hierarchically the structure design principle of the heterogenous cyberphysical systems is shown. Finally, the cyberattacks can lead to unpredictable phenomena where the space system is in non-nominal conditions, so the modeling phase shall include also non-linear cases. Fig. 5 shows the

Section evidence: The procedure described until now belongs to the causal-modeling approach. Because of the involvement of different CubeSat subsystems in a complex Multiphysics domain, the A-causal method can be useful to simplify the modeling part. In fact, according to this method, the modeling is more focused on the physical connections (connectors or ports) between parts rather than on their interaction in terms of input and output. "There are no input and output variables in real life" (Dr. Yaman Barlas). Fig. 4 shows this difference of modeling approach in the electric domain (capacitor object) using OpenModelica against Simulink language. It is worthy to notice how: in

the first case, there is the definition of the elementary port (physical connection), the non-flow variable (voltage), the flow-variable (current), the constitutive and connection equations; on the contrary in the Simulink case, there is the direct translation of the mathematical model where the voltage is assumed as input and the current as output (losing the physical meaning).

caption_chunks.context: To create a model from an existing DSM representation, the first step was to make the DSM symmetric by assuming any interaction to be bidirectional, a simplifying assumption given that it is not clear if a directional flow would reduce the interaction complexity. The interactions between parts of different subsystems were depicted as interactions between the subsystem themselves. caption_chunks.context: CSM is a COTS multi-platform collaborative MBSE environment, which delivers intelligence, robustness and creativity to define, track and visualize all aspects of systems in the most standard-compliant SysML models and diagrams (Cameo Systems Modeler, n.d.). In this thesis paper, the version for the CSM is 19.0 SP1 enterprise edition and operating system is Windows 10. The reasons for choosing CSM are as follows- most widely used SysML tool in the industry, ADSL lab have the commercial license for CSM and CSM comes with Cameo Simulation Toolkit (CST) plugin. CST plugin is helpful for validating system behavior and model checking by executing, animating and debugging SysML diagrams, which are made executable. other_visible_labels: The SSA system shall be available 24/7/365.
The SSA system shall continue to operate regardless of component failure but may degrade performance.
The SSA system shall provide equal or greater than 99 percent SSA Relevance.
The SSA system shall threshold measures of effectiveness with up to 20% sensors failed/not available.
The SSA system shall operate autonomously.
Human Operator input shall always override SSA system autonomous operations.
The SSA system shall track all objects greater than 25 cubic centimeters within 36,000 kilometers of the earth's surface.
The SSA system shall continuously project forward the paths of all tracked space objects 24 hours and notify of any projected collisions or near misses within that period.

The SSA system shall project forward the results of each projected collision and a projected near miss as if it was a collision, individually, collectively, and upon operator request any proper subset for three (3) months.
The SSA system shall provide an interpretation of any action taken including recommended course of action within 30 seconds of said action.

The SSA system shall continuously provide three (3) estimates of the situation designated 1) most likely, 2) possible, and 3) least likely including likelihood of occurrence, likelihood of aggressive action, and action predicted for every space-faring nation in the next four (4) hours for each estimate.

caption_chunks.context: In this scenario, a CubeSat namely "ADSLSat" is created using classical coordinates. By utilizing the AdvCAT object of STK, potential close proximity and encounters between "ADSLSat" and other two-line element (TLE) sets have been calculated. The scenario resides under Behavior->System Behavior Simulation package in the CubeSat-SSA system model and can be run through an executable SysML state machine diagram. System context for this scenario is "Close Approach". The scenario automatically produces two reports namely "Close Approach By Min Range" and "Encounter Warnings". The reports are also saved in separate Excel files which can be reincorporated into the model through excel sync capability of cameo simulation toolkit. Figure 4.15 shows the interaction between CSM, STK and Excel for Scenario 2.

caption_chunks.caption: Figure 4.15: Interaction between CSM, STK and Excel for scenario 2
caption_chunks.context: In this scenario, a CubeSat namely "ADSLSat" is created using classical coordinates. By utilizing the AdvCAT object of STK, potential close proximity and encounters between "ADSLSat" and other two-line element (TLE) sets have been calculated. The scenario resides under Behavior->System Behavior Simulation package in the CubeSat-SSA system model and can be run through an executable SysML state machine diagram. System context for this scenario is "Close Approach". The scenario automatically produces two reports namely "Close Approach By Min Range" and "Encounter Warnings". The reports are also saved in separate Excel files which can be reincorporated into the model through excel sync capability of cameo simulation toolkit. Figure 4.15 shows the interaction between CSM, STK and Excel for Scenario 2.

caption_chunks.context: The FireSAT mission was aimed at observing forest fires $ ^{35} $ and has been adopted as a standard study case for understanding the space SD process. caption_chunks.caption: FIGURE 18 Top level activity diagram of FFSMCS
caption_chunks.context: Although a conventional MBSD approach can specify components and parameters realizing functions of the mission by iterative processes, function analysis resulting in unsatisfactory requirements due to the omission of potential relationships between functions, behaviors, components, and requirements should be determined. Especially when functions are coupled, designers have to reselect DPs, and even reanalyze FRs, which dramatically increases iteration times and obstructs development efficiency. The proposed A-MBSD is thus applied to the FFSMCS to illustrate how the RFBS documents SD information explicitly helping designers to make decisions through building design matrixes and using the Independence Axiom.

The stereotype package holds all domain-specific stereotypes (VLC system stereotypes) which are extended from the UML and SysML meta-classes. A VLC stereotype specializes a SysML stereotype. Section evidence: A key MBSE challenge is to develop and maintain a unique model of the system, from the earliest stages of system development. This model can then continuously evolve through the lifecycle: formulation, design, manufacturing, and operations. This unique model would serve as the "blueprint" of the system. This challenge is addressed by SLIM (Systems LIfecycle Management), a vision concept and software environment developed by InterCAX. [29][30][31] SLIM enables systems engineers to develop a high-level system model in SysML and connect it to domain-specific models, such as Bills of Materials (BOMs) and Computer Aided Design (CAD), Computer Aided Engineering (CAE), MATLAB/Simulink, and Mathematica documents, managed in various enterprise product lifecycle management systems, such as Teamcenter (Siemens Project Lifecycle Management (PLM)) and Windchill (PTC). SLIM manages these fine-grained connections to various versions

of the models and can sync data or generate/sync complete model structures. In the context of the CubeSat work, we exercised the following use cases with SLIM:

(1) Use Case 1: Develop an initial architecture of the CubeSat in SysML and automatically generate a part structure in a PLM system which becomes a starting point for mechanical/electrical designers for further decomposing the parts and developing Mechanical and Electrical CAD models.

caption_chunks.context: This work is a key part of the INCOSE MBSE Initiative's Systems Engineering Vision 2020 [1]. MBSE is the formalized application of modeling to support system requirements, design, analysis, optimization, verification, and validation. It begins in the conceptual design phase, continuing throughout development and into later life cycle phases including operations. A high-level overview describing the relationship between MBSE and SysML is provided in Figure 1. The MBSE Initiative started at the January 2007 INCOSE International Workshop [2]. The MBSE Roadmap was created to define the high-level, long term vision for the maturation and acceptance of MBSE across academia and industry.

caption_chunks.context: The overall concept for the methodology is shown in Figure 1. Preliminary scoping and requirements analysis are used to define a manageable exploration problem. The objective for the exploration is the expected value of producing a particular architecture, based on the revenue of successfully completing a mission minus the cost of the aggregate system. This will be more thoroughly discussed in Sections A-C. The tradespace for the problem is captured using the SysML modeling language (described in Section D). Finally, the automated trade space exploration (described in Section E) takes the objective function, mission requirements, and scoped trade space as inputs and then generates and evaluates a large number of potential cellularized architectures.

caption_chunks.context: The dynamic behaviour of a satellite in LEO is typically non-linear over a number of length-scales. For example, environmental perturbations contribute to secular variation in the orbital dynamics over periods of days and months, motion of the satellite about the earth occurs over minutes and data collection and transmission can take place over a period of seconds. Within this work the long-term dynamics are captured in a Lifetime model, which conducts analysis over the complete mission, whilst dynamics related to the other two scales are analysed over a number of orbits within an Operations model, consisting of higher detail and fidelity. caption_chunks.context: The SysML Internal Block Diagram, in Figure 5, provides the basis for modeling both the propagation of radio waves and also the trapping of ionospheric particles. Each aspect of the Earth's atmosphere has different effects on the propagation of radio waves. Water vapor is primarily concentrated in the troposphere and absorbs radio waves at various frequencies. The ionosphere contains charged elements that interact with radio waves. Both these factors influence the transmission of communication signals between the satellite and ground station. It also contains the primary science target of the mission: a series of trapped plasma formations.

caption_chunks.context: Fig. 1: Inter-dependencies between Architectural model and Operational model. and space mission design. This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the proposed operational scenario modeling coupled with architectural definition; while Section 3 compares the two case studies as an end-to-end validation of the proposed methodology. Section 4 discusses the main outcomes of this work and lessons learned. Finally, Section 5 summarizes the proposed work and provides directions for future work. 2 Proposed Operations modeling This section presents a modeling approach for ConOps and OMs as integral part of the system architecture modeling within the newly developed Modeling & Simulation Architecture for integrated Complex systems (MOSAiC) MBSE framework [11, 19]. The methodology builds upon the ARCADIA method and uses the Capella toolset, while proposing the co-development of system behavior and architecture through formal abstractions and state-based modeling. Unlike conventional practices where to the authors' best knowledge mostly only architectural models are developed, the proposed approach establishes a continuous and traceable linkage between system structure and mission execution logic, ensuring consistency throughout the lifecycle. 2.1 Methodological Foundations The modeling process follows ARCADIA's layered abstraction, beginning with Operational Analysis (OA), which defines mission goals and stakeholder interactions, and advancing through System Analysis (SA), Logical Architecture (LA), and Physical Architecture (PA) [4]. At each stage, the architecture is incrementally refined - from functional groupings to subsystem allocations and finally to component - level instantiations. ConOps elements are modeled concurrently with this structural development. Mission phases - such as launch, commissioning, or nominal operations - define the operational timeline. Within each phase, the system may adopt different internal configurations or behaviors - captured as Operating Modes. These OMs, defined through Capella's state machine diagrams, represent both the system's status (e.g., Safe Mode, Science Mode) and the conditions under which transitions occur (e.g., power thresholds, visibility events, fault recovery). At the subsystem level, Modes represent variations in functional behavior (e.g., Payload Active, TTC Idle) based on the current mission phase and system objectives. Using add-ons like the Property Values Management Tool (PVMT) [20] within Capella, quantitative data such as power consumption and relative margins are assigned to components and subsystems based on their active mode. These parameters are crucial for performance simulations and for assessing the validity of operational scenarios within design constraints. The tight coupling between state-based logic and physical properties allows designers to directly simulate mission execution and verify design compliance at early stages $ ^{1} $ $ ^{1} $All data and models are available in a public repository under GPLv3 license at [19].

caption_chunks.context: 2.2 Interconnection Between Architectural and Operational Models The core of the proposed methodology is its emphasis on the interconnection between the architectural and operational models. This relationship is captured in a layered model framework (see Fig. 1), which illustrates how operational definitions and architectural abstractions evolve in parallel, influencing and constraining one another across the system lifecycle. On the architectural side, the model progresses from OA through SA, LA, and PA. Each level introduces greater design specificity - from abstract functions to logical subsystems to physical components. In parallel, the operational model introduces corresponding layers of behavioral detail: from broad ConOps phases to detailed system modes and subsystem-level variations. This bidirectional structure supports both design derivation and behavioral execution. The required operations "drive the design of" the architecture by defining available capabilities and constraints; conversely, the architectural elements "execute" the operations, activating specific functions and behaviors in time. For instance, an OM such as "Science Acquisition" will dictate the active configuration of subsystems, turning on payload components, activating data storage, and powering down nonessential services. These behavioral requirements must be anticipated and satisfied by the architectural layout defined at the LA and PA levels. Capella enables this integration through explicit cross-model references. OMs are not modeled in isolation; rather, they are embedded in the same environment as architectural elements, allowing mode-specific behavior to be tied directly to component definitions and mission scenarios. Transitions between modes (and thus different behaviors that a component might have) are governed by environmental or system triggers - visibility conditions, battery levels, or ground station access and reflect the actual execution environment of the spacecraft. Because these transitions are stored alongside component-level data and system structure, simulations can leverage the complete model for performance assessment. 3 Case studies comparison 3.1 Satellite Case Study To validate this integrated modeling methodology, it was firstly applied to the FIRE-EYE mission - a multisatellite CubeSat constellation designed for near-realtime wildfire monitoring in the Mediterranean region, already presented in a preparatory work [11]. The mission was selected as a representative case due to its operational complexity, resource constraints, and need for mode-driven autonomy across multiple mission phases. The system consists of 48 16U CubeSats equipped with multi-spectral imaging payloads. Each satellite operates autonomously and undergoes a structured lifecycle composed of launch, commissioning, nominal operation, science acquisition, and data transmission phases. These phases were modeled as discrete ConOps stages, each linked to specific OMs that reflected the system's intended behavior. In the OA phase, the primary stakeholders - including civil protection agencies, regional authorities, and the mission operators - were modeled with their associated operational capabilities, as shown in Fig. 2. Fig. 2: Main project capabilities and Stakeholders identification A primary operational capability was identified to represent the mission goal: [SCI-OBJ] To near-realtime monitor wildfire in the Mediterranean area. This capability encompasses the system's core function of detecting, mapping, and alerting wildfire events with minimal latency. In parallel, a second capability was defined: [STANDARD] Mission Lifecycle, which represents the set of standardized processes and lifecycle phases required to design, develop, launch, operate, and dispose of the space segment. This capability supports alignment with established space mission development practices (e.g., ECSS standards) and enables long-term roadmapping. Subsequently, stakeholder activities and interactions were modeled to clarify user needs and objectives, as shown in Fig. 3. The Capella OA enables the creation of a domain model - abstracted from the future system to focus on the stakeholders' real-world needs, independently of any technical implementation [21]. Fig. 3: FireEYE Operational Architecture. These activities, such as "to detect wildfires" or "to provide alerts and situational awareness", were used to drive the system analysis and function breakdown.

Another key result is the generalization of Operating Modes (OMs) for CubeSats by identifying common attributes and transition criteria among different Low Earth Orbit (LEO) CubeSat Concepts of Operations (ConOps's). This allows mission scenarios to be defined by modifying OM attributes, regardless of the data format. Additionally, a specialized parser created for model files allows for automatic updates to the model itself, such as after simulation or parameter optimization phases. A proof of concept is demonstrated using the SysML model of the "The White Compass (TWC)" theoretical mission, integrated with the Nanostar Software Suite (NSS) [12, 13] analysis tools through a dedicated parser, successfully producing power and data budgets $ ^{1} $ . 3 Systems and Unified Modelling Languages The Unified Modelling Language (UML) [14], developed in the late 1980s and early 1990s, quickly became a leading modeling language, primarily used for software development [15]. In the early 2000s, the Systems Modelling Language (SysML) [16] was introduced by the Object Management Group (OMG), International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE), and other collaborators as a specialized extension of UML tailored for Systems Engineering applications, particularly for modeling complex physical systems. A comprehensive discussion of SE methodologies with SysML can be found in Weilkiens [15]. Key concepts from UML and SysML that are critical to understanding this work are outlined below. 3.1 UML Classes A core element of object-oriented modeling, classes define both the structure and behavior of objects that share similar characteristics. Classes are characterized by their attributes (structure) and operations (behavior) and are represented through class diagrams. These diagrams can depict software components or real-world objects, at varying levels of abstraction [15]. Fig. 2: Example of a UML class and object, illustrating inherited attributes and operations. Attributes Attributes specify the properties that define a model, which classes inherit. These properties include visibility, name, type, and multiplicity (the number of instances associated with each class) [15]. Associations Associations describe relationships between two classes. Types of associations include aggregation (which represents a whole-part hierarchy) and composition (a whole-part hierarchy where parts cannot exist independently of the whole) [15]. Generalizations Generalizations create hierarchies between a general superclass and a more specific subclass [15]. The subclass represents a more specialized form of the superclass (e.g., cat, dog, and horse are subclasses of the animal superclass) .

caption_chunks.context: Fig. 3: Example of UML generalization. Stereotypes Stereotypes allow the extension of existing model elements by introducing new properties and/or behaviors. The keyword > is used to indicate the base element that is being extended [15]. (a) (b) Fig. 4: Examples of UML stereotypes. (a) Example of stereotype definition. (b) Example of stereotype application. 3.2 SysML Blocks and Block Definition Diagrams In SysML, UML classes are referred to as blocks, and UML class diagrams are represented as Block Definition Diagrams (BDDs). SysML expands the scope of UML classes, enabling the modeling of system structures across multiple domains beyond software [15]. Value Types, Units, and Dimensions A value type is a specialized form of UML data type that includes both a unit and a dimension. Units describe the physical measurement units, while dimensions specify the quantities associated with those units [15]. Requirements and Requirement Diagrams SysML introduces the concept of requirements, which define the conditions that a system must satisfy. These are illustrated in requirement diagrams [15]. 4 Stereotypes application Several studies (e.g., Bajaj et al. [17] and Spangelo et al. [18]) have introduced tools that attempt to address some of the integration challenges between SysML models and domain-specific simulation tools. Specifically, they enable SysML models to interface with specialized simulation environments, thereby streamlining the design and analysis process. Such works, while providing useful information about the use of SysML as an interface between external databases and external simulation tools, require the use of proprietary tools. Two main requirements have been imposed for the formalization presented in [9]: the exclusive use of open-source tools, following the principle of Open Science, and the use of a single model, inclusive of all mission parameters to facilitate the PD phase of a CubeSat without the need to refer to an external database. In the meantime, the demand for an open-source CubeSat design resulted in several initiatives, e.g.: the Libre Space Foundation [19]: University of Patras Satellite (UPSat) [20]; LibreCube [21]; Satellite Networked Open Ground Stations (SatNOGS) [22]; ArduSat [23]; Open Source CubeSat Workshop [24]; Nanostar Software Suite (NSS) [12, 13]. To the best of the authors' knowledge, however, no open-source framework existed that fully addressed all the challenges and requirements outlined in this research. The question to be answered by the proposed formalization was then whether it was possible to use MBSE as a frontend for the entire design cycle of a CubeSat, with the exclusive use of open-source tools. With this in mind, SysML has been chosen as principal modeling language for the proposed formalization, given its strengths and benefits, discussed thoroughly e.g. in Weilkiens [15] or Holt and Perry [25]. However, despite its robust modeling capabilities, SysML does not inherently offer the specific, quantifiable data required for simulation and analysis, as analyzed in [11]. Critical elements such as mass, power consumption of system components, and orbital parameters are essential for accurate simulations and system budgeting. To address this limitation, currently simulation tools must be fed with external mathematical databases that provide the detailed data necessary for these tasks.

caption_chunks.context: SysML elements, such as the above-mentioned Requirements and Blocks, are derived by applying stereotypes to existing UML elements, such as classes, making the SysML a specialization of the UML. An analogous approach has then been introduced for the proposed formalization, which therefore can be interpreted as a specialization of the SysML for CubeSats design activities. Through the introduction of several stereotypes, it becomes possible to specialize the SysML Block element into System, Component, Orbit, GroundStation or OperatingMode new elements, each one of them inheriting a standardized set of attributes for their characterization. An example of the Orbit element included with the proposed formalization is shown in Fig. 5. Fig. 5: Orbit UML stereotype example [9]. As shown in the Figure, it is created by applying a new stereotype to the UML Class «metaclass» - from which also the SysML Block element is originated - through an Extension $ ^{2} $ Relationship. By introducing such a stereotype, the designer can create any desired Orbit element by adding the appropriate values to the pre-defined set of attributes that the element will inherit (i.e., in this instance, the orbital parameters). More generally, once the stereotypes are incorporated into the model, they can be reused for various designs by simply adjusting the input data. Moreover, this approach does not limit the modeling capabilities of the SysML, since it is still possible to generate any desired element, diagram or connection in the model or to directly use the new elements in various diagrams like "classical" Blocks - without affecting the correctness of the model itself. 5 Discussion The application of UML stereotypes within the proposed formalization of the CubeSat SysML model provides several critical advantages that enhance the design process, data management, and overall efficiency of CubeSat development. These advantages are discussed throughout this section. One of the primary benefits of using this approach lies in the ability to create models that are both reusable and flexible. In the formalization proposed in [9], the stereotypes are designed to be generic yet sufficiently detailed to represent various CubeSat configurations. Once the stereotypes are integrated into the model, they can be reused across multiple designs without needing to recreate the structure or redefine attributes. Designers only need to update the specific data points, such as mass or power consumption, to reflect changes in the design or mission requirements. This flexibility is particularly valuable as iterative design processes are common, and multiple CubeSat missions may be developed simultaneously or sequentially. By maintaining a standardized framework using UML stereotypes, teams can reduce the time spent on manual model adjustments and focus on refining mission-specific details. Furthermore, the use of UML stereotypes facilitates identifying common structures in the model files, enabling the extraction of critical data for integration with any preferred set of simulation tools. This integration is achieved through the use of a dedicated parser, which leverages on the information conveyed by the stereotypes. Moreover, the parser - by knowing in advance the set of stereotypes and therefore the attributes introduced with them - automatically extracts the relevant data from the elements of the SysML model with a specific stereotype applied and converts them into a software-readable format. This reduces the risk of data fragmentation or inconsistencies across different tools and phases of the design process, ensuring that the CubeSat model remains the single source of truth throughout the PD phase without limiting the broader modeling capabilities of SysML, since it uses only the information relative to the stereotypes for data extraction, bypassing all other model's elements. The proposed set of stereotypes facilitates the automation of data extraction from the CubeSat model, streamlining the process of generating system budgets, performing trade-off studies, and conducting simulations. Once the relevant system parameters are defined using stereotypes, the model can be parsed to extract critical data such as: power consumptions, and mass estimates. This eliminates the need for manual data entry on each simulation tool, reducing the possibility of human error and significantly speeding up the design process. Moreover, the approach supports bidirectional data flow, meaning that updates from simulation results or parameter optimizations can be fed back into the SysML model automatically. For example, if a simulation tool determines an optimized power consumption profile, this data can be updated in the model without manual intervention. This automated update capability supports an agile and responsive design process, where the model is contin

With the same principles used for data extraction, the use of stereotypes in the formalization also supports the generation of dependency graphs as the one shown in Fig. 6, which visually depict the relationships between different system components and how changes in one parameter (e.g., mass or power consumption) affect other parts of the system. By knowing in advance the relationship between the data included within the stereotypes (e.g., system's power consumption and OMs overall power consumption), and by reading in the SysML the connections between the elements with specific stereotypes applied (e.g., composite associations between components and main systems), the data extraction process can automatically generate these graphs, which are particularly valuable for conducting trade-off studies during the PD phase. For example, the graph in Fig. 6 shows the connection between the masses of specific components and the Payload's overall mass, as well as the one between the system's power consumption and the consumptions of some OMs. Dependency graphs help designers understand the interdependencies within the CubeSat system and evaluate the impact of design changes. For example, increasing the power consumption of a system may require adjustments to the power budget, battery capacity, or solar array specifications. By visualizing these dependencies, designers can make more informed decisions and optimize system performance while managing trade-offs between competing design constraints. The integration of UML stereotypes into the CubeSat model also aligns with CE practices by supporting realtime collaboration among multidisciplinary teams. With the standardized data structure provided by stereotypes, different teams (e.g., power systems, communications, thermal management) can work concurrently on the same model, ensuring that their contributions are integrated seamlessly. The automated data extraction and update features also allow for continuous synchronization between the design model and simulation results, fostering a more dynamic and collaborative design process. While using stereotypes in the CubeSat SysML model formalization offers advantages, there are also some drawbacks and limitations. One of the primary drawbacks is the dependency on specific modeling tools, as discussed in Pons et al. [26]. The current framework was developed using Gaphor [27], an open-source modeling tool, and the parser designed for data extraction is tailored specifically to this tool. This creates limitations in terms of interoperability with other SysML tools, such as Papyrus [28] or Capella [29], which may store or structure their model files differently. As a result, the parser would require significant modification to be compatible with other tools, making the framework less flexible for users who prefer or are required to use different SysML platforms. This limitation reduces the broader applicability of the formalization, especially in environments where multiple tools are used or where teams need to switch between tools due to organizational requirements or project-specific needs. A temporary limitation is that the framework is focused solely on LEO CubeSat missions at the time being. Making it less suitable for complex missions involving non-nominal conditions, such as Early Orbit Phase (EOP) or off-nominal scenarios (e.g., detumbling or calibration). Customization for specialized missions can be time-consuming, especially when new stereotypes are required for novel subsystems, increasing the complexity of the model. The success of the approach heavily depends on the accuracy of the initial SysML model. Any inaccuracies or omissions can propagate through the system, leading to flawed simulations or incorrect system budgets. This necessitates thorough validation of the model, increasing the workload in the design phase. For larger teams, inconsistent application of stereotypes can cause data fragmentation, leading to synchronization issues across subsystems and complicating system-wide analyses. caption_chunks.context: 2.2 Model Based Systems Engineering Model-based systems engineering, or MBSE, is the formalized application of modeling to support tasks of a systems engineer including activities related to requirements, design, analysis, validation, and verification. This work begins in the conceptual design phase and continues on throughout development and later life cycle phases. [3] Figure 1 shows the phases of a typical design and the tasks which MBSE often aids in. Figure 1: MBSE across the System Life Cycle [3] MBSE is a term that describes an approach to Systems Engineering that emphasizes a system architecture model as the primary work artifact throughout the system development life cycle. A model is an approximation, representation, or idealization of selected aspects of the structure, behavior, or operation of a real world process, concept, or system. [4] A model usually offers different views in order to serve different purposes. A view is a representation of a system from the perspective of related concerns or issues. MBSE combines traditional systems engineering best practices with rigorous visual modeling techniques. Systems Engineers must interface with various other engineering specialties

caption_chunks.context: Figure 4: PolySat team member holds CP-6 mission [9] CubeSat missions can cost anywhere from fifty thousand dollars for a low-end satellite with limited functionality, up to multi-million dollars for a high-end satellite with multiple mission goals and associated instruments. The lower end of the spectrum is far below all other satellite design costs and has made the CubeSat a viable option for schools and universities across the world. Because of this, a large number of universities and some companies and government organizations around the world are developing CubeSats. A common design approach for CubeSat mission planning is to learn from previous design team knowledge and use intuition based trade studies for mission design. This can be dangerous if key personnel are unavailable, or operational parameters are neglected in the early stages of design. This often leads to cost and scheduling overruns, intolerable for a low budget CubeSat mission. However, these risks can be mitigated if standardized design practices, such as SysML, and standardized trade templates, such as HSF, are in place. Section evidence: In order to promote the development of the tool chain and improve the convenience of data interaction between tools, the tool chain adopts a unified Eclipse-based plug-in development platform, shown in Fig. 4. The platform is divided into three layers. The top layer is the application development platform that enables the development of specific functions of the tool. The middle layer is the core tool platform, which includes the implementation of meta-model, model analysis, model comparison, basic project management, etc. The bottom layer is the Eclipse platform, which is a scalable open source multi-function system that integrates the program development platform, run time environment and application framework [33]. The tool chain integrates tools and related plug-ins in the form of plug-in on the Eclipse platform. In addition, the tool chain can dynamically call some mature software to assists the function, such as MATLAB/Simulink, C/C++ development tool (CDT), STK, etc.

Section evidence: A case is showed in Fig. 11, which demonstrates the development process of the tool chain platform. The case is about the SDR system model in the SDR SOC. This paper integrates SIMULINK's Target Language Compiler code generation tool on the Eclipse platform to automatically generate the internal behavior code of the component. This part of the code is platform independent. After the SDR system model is built in the Graphics editing area and the internal algorithm is designed, based on the principle of Velocity template engine, the second phase of target language compilation is carried out. With the software component description file and the hardware platform description file, the system configuration tool generates .c and .h code files, and finally the target file is compiled. The executable file can be download to the target board to test its function. From the platform independent code to the specific platform code, the Velocity template engine first maps the template, that is, the internal component code, to the hardware interface, and then reflects the configuration parameters in the code. All other components can be developed and executed in accordance with this process.

The use cases are elaborated below.

Section evidence: A key MBSE challenge is to develop and maintain a unique model of the system, from the earliest stages of system development. This model can then continuously evolve through the lifecycle: formulation, design, manufacturing, and operations. This unique model would serve as the "blueprint" of the system. This challenge is addressed by SLIM (Systems LIfecycle Management), a vision concept and software environment developed by InterCAX. [29][30][31] SLIM enables systems engineers to develop a high-level system model in SysML and connect it to domain-specific models, such as Bills of Materials (BOMs) and Computer Aided Design (CAD), Computer Aided Engineering (CAE), MATLAB/Simulink, and Mathematica documents, managed in various enterprise product lifecycle management systems, such as Teamcenter (Siemens Project Lifecycle Management (PLM)) and Windchill (PTC). SLIM manages these fine-grained connections to various versions

of the models and can sync data or generate/sync complete model structures. In the context of the CubeSat work, we exercised the following use cases with SLIM:

(1) Use Case 1: Develop an initial architecture of the CubeSat in SysML and automatically generate a part structure in a PLM system which becomes a starting point for mechanical/electrical designers for further decomposing the parts and developing Mechanical and Electrical CAD models.

Abstract—Satellites and other complex systems now become more and more software dependent. Even nanosatellites have complexity that can be compared to scientific instruments launched to Mars. COTS components and subsystems may now be purchased to support payload development. On the contrary, the software has to be adapted to the new payload and, consequently, hardware architecture selected for the satellite. There is not a rigorous and robust way to design software for CubeSats or small satellites yet. In this paper, we will briefly review some existing systems and present our approach, which based on Behaviour-Interaction-Priority (BIP) framework. We will describe our experience in implementing fight software simulation and testing in the Swiss CubETH CubeSat project. We will conclude with lessons learned and future utilization of BIP for hardware testing and simulation.

Here we present our approach using the Behaviour- Interaction-Priority (BIP) framework [4], a component-based language which can be used to build correct-by-construction applications. It has been developed by the Verimag laboratory in Grenoble university and is currently used in the EPFL by the Rigorous System Design laboratory (RISD). BIP can be used to formally model complex systems and provides a toolset for their verification and validation and for code generation. The framework is young; therefore there are not many practical designs with it yet.

Modular nature of the BIP approach allows iterative design for satellites in development and adaptation to hardware changes. In order to accomplish modularity, common patterns in components and structures have to be developed. The verification of the correctness in the BIP model is made by using a set of common rules in the assembly of atoms and compounds.

We have used the BIP approach in the our CubeSat project (CubETH) to design logic for the operation of a satellite and compiled into machine code, which was executed on the onboard computer. Software running Control and Data Management system compiled for Cortex-A3 processor design. This work has proven technical feasibility and exposed a number of problems with the approach. Our next goal is to develop a visual environment to provide graphical user interface to simplify generation of the BIP code.

In this work we will present main principles of the BIP framework, our implementation, and challenges for implementation on a CubeSat platform.

In the international standards for architecture description and software engineering a number of quality attributes is specified as expression of "ilities" - qualities such as reliability, portability, modularity and others. Software designed with these qualities in mind is more robust to faults in hardware. At the European level, these attributes are described in a set of European Cooperation for Space (ECSS) standards, such as [8]. At NASA, in addition to standard design practices a recent effort [9] has been underway to specify a large table of quality attributes for mission flight software. In this work, we would like to concentrate primarily on robustness, safety, modularity and portability qualities for flight software architectures for nano and mico satellites and scientific instruments.

Abstract—Satellites and other complex systems now become more and more software dependent. Even nanosatellites have complexity that can be compared to scientific instruments launched to Mars. COTS components and subsystems may now be purchased to support payload development. On the contrary, the software has to be adapted to the new payload and, consequently, hardware architecture selected for the satellite. There is not a rigorous and robust way to design software for CubeSats or small satellites yet. In this paper, we will briefly review some existing systems and present our approach, which based on Behaviour-Interaction-Priority (BIP) framework. We will describe our experience in implementing fight software simulation and testing in the Swiss CubETH CubeSat project. We will conclude with lessons learned and future utilization of BIP for hardware testing and simulation.

Here we present our approach using the Behaviour- Interaction-Priority (BIP) framework [4], a component-based language which can be used to build correct-by-construction applications. It has been developed by the Verimag laboratory in Grenoble university and is currently used in the EPFL by the Rigorous System Design laboratory (RISD). BIP can be used to formally model complex systems and provides a toolset for their verification and validation and for code generation. The framework is young; therefore there are not many practical designs with it yet.

Modular nature of the BIP approach allows iterative design for satellites in development and adaptation to hardware changes. In order to accomplish modularity, common patterns in components and structures have to be developed. The verification of the correctness in the BIP model is made by using a set of common rules in the assembly of atoms and compounds.

We have used the BIP approach in the our CubeSat project (CubETH) to design logic for the operation of a satellite and compiled into machine code, which was executed on the onboard computer. Software running Control and Data Management system compiled for Cortex-A3 processor design. This work has proven technical feasibility and exposed a number of problems with the approach. Our next goal is to develop a visual environment to provide graphical user interface to simplify generation of the BIP code.

In this work we will present main principles of the BIP framework, our implementation, and challenges for implementation on a CubeSat platform.

Therefore, combined application of architectures can generate deadlocks. We have used the DFinder tool [13] to verify deadlock-freedom of the case study model. DFinder applies compositional verification on BIP models by overapproximating the set of reachable states and checking symbolically that the intersection of the obtained set and the set of deadlock states is empty. This approach allows DFinder to analyse very large models. The tool is sound, but incomplete: due to the above mentioned over-approximation it can produce false positives, i.e. potential deadlock states that are unreachable in the concrete system. However, our case study model was shown to be deadlock-free without any potential deadlocks.

Report evidence: The early validation of requirements aims to reduce the need for the high-cost validation testing and corrective measures at late development stages. This work introduces a systematic process for the unambiguous specification of system requirements and the guided derivation of formal properties, which should be implied by the system 's structure and behavior in conjunction with its external stimuli. This rigorous design takes place through the incremental construction of a model using the BIP (Behavior-Interaction-Priorities) component framework. It allows building complex designs by composing simpler reusable designs enforcing given properties. If some properties are neither enforced nor verified, the model is refined or certain requirements are revised. A validated model provides evidence of requirements' consistency and design correctness. The process is semi-automated through a new tool and existing verification tools. Its effectiveness was evaluated on a set of requirements for the control software of the CubETH nanosatellite and an extract of software requirements for a Low Earth Orbit observation satellite. Our experience and obtained results helped in identifying open challenges for applying the method in industrial context. These challenges concern with the domain knowledge representation, the expressiveness of used specification languages, the library of reusable designs and scalability.

caption_chunks.context:
Although the architecture in Figure 4 can be applied to precisely two components, it is clear that an architecture of the same style—with n parameter components and 2n connectors—could be applied to n operand components satisfying the interface assumptions. We specify such architecture styles with architecture diagrams [52]. An architecture diagram consists of a set of component types with cardinality constraints for the expected number of instances and a set of connector motifs. Connector motifs are non-empty sets of port types. Each port type has a cardinality constraint representing the expected number of port instances per component and two additional constraints: multiplicity and degree, represented as a pair m:d. Additionally, each port type is typed as either trigger or synchron.
